procedural_history.originating_court: Not explicitly stated, but the case originated with FIR No. 375/2022 dated 31.10.2022, implying a police station within the jurisdiction of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 19.07.2023 passed in CRM-M-34512-2023 by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellants filed CRM-M-34512-2023 before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh seeking to quash FIR No. 375/2022. The High Court refused to quash the FIR.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants, aggrieved by the High Court's refusal to quash the FIR, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The Impugned Order is set aside.
The entire criminal proceedings arising out of the Subject FIR are quashed and set aside.
This order shall not have any effect on the Civil Suit pending between the parties and the same shall be decided in accordance with law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on the ground that the dispute was essentially civil in nature and a civil remedy was already being pursued.

facts: The appellants were accused in an F.I.R. registered for offences including cheating and forgery.
The dispute originated from a commercial transaction involving a sale deed for a property.
The appellants had already filed a civil suit concerning the property and their lawful possession, which was pending.
Subsequently, the complainant (Respondent No. 2) registered the F.I.R. against the appellants.
The appellants filed a petition under Section 482 of the CrPC before the High Court to quash the F.I.R., arguing the dispute was civil in nature, but the High Court refused.
The appellants then appealed this refusal to the Supreme Court.
law: Under Section 482 of the CrPC, the High Court has the inherent power to quash criminal proceedings to prevent the abuse of the process of court or to secure the ends of justice.
This power must be used cautiously and sparingly.
The High Court must determine if a dispute that is essentially civil in nature has been given a "cloak of criminal offence."

If a civil remedy is available and is already being pursued for a dispute that is primarily civil, the High Court should not hesitate to quash the criminal proceedings to prevent an abuse of the court's process.
application: The Supreme Court found that the core dispute between the parties was "entirely civil in nature," revolving around the validity of a sale deed and the lawful possession of the property.
It noted that the appellants had already taken the appropriate step of filing a civil suit to resolve this very issue.

The Court identified several factors indicating that the complainant was attempting to shroud a civil dispute with a "cloak of criminality": the F.I.R. was filed only after the appellants had initiated the civil suit, the complainant selectively implicated the appellants, and the appellants had demonstrated good faith by previously paying rent.
The Court reasoned that the substance of the criminal complaint merely served to cast doubt on a commercial transaction, an issue that was already before the Civil Court.
Therefore, allowing the criminal proceedings to continue would amount to an abuse of the process of the court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred. It held that when a dispute is essentially civil, and a civil remedy is already being pursued, the High Court ought to have quashed the criminal proceedings. The Court found that the criminal complaint was an attempt to give a cloak of criminality to a civil dispute and was an abuse of the process of law. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and quashed the criminal proceedings against the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in refusing to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on the ground that the dispute was essentially civil in nature and a civil remedy was already being pursued.
appellant_arguments: The dispute between the parties is essentially civil in nature.
The criminal proceedings amount to an abuse of the process of law because an appropriate civil remedy is already being pursued by the appellants.
The High Court erred by not considering the litigation history between the parties, which includes a pending Civil Suit and an FIR filed by the appellants against the respondent's family.
Given that a civil remedy was already being pursued, the High Court should have quashed the criminal proceedings.
respondent_arguments: There is sufficient prima facie evidence for the Trial Court to proceed against the appellants.
The mere existence of a civil dispute does not justify the quashing of criminal proceedings.
Respondent No. 2 (the private party) did not contest the matter before the Supreme Court.

cases.case_name: Paramjeet Batra v. State of Uttarakhand
cases.principle: To expound on the scope of the exercise of power under Section 482 CrPC.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a dispute is essentially civil in nature but is given the cloak of a criminal offense, and a civil remedy is available and is being pursued, the High Court should quash the criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to prevent an abuse of the process of the court.
obiter: The High Court's power under Section 482 of the Code is to be used cautiously and sparingly to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
Whether a complaint discloses a criminal offense depends on the nature of the facts alleged, and the High Court must judge if the essential ingredients are present.
A complaint that discloses civil transactions may also have a criminal texture.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court ought to have quashed the criminal proceedings when it was apprised of the fact that the substance of the Criminal Complaint served only a cast of doubt on the validity of a commercial transaction and an appropriate civil remedy was already being pursued.
legal_tests_applied: When exercising jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code, the High Court must see whether a dispute which is essentially of a civil nature is given a cloak of criminal offence. In such a situation, if a civil remedy is available and is, in fact, adopted, the High Court should not hesitate to quash criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of process of court.
policy_considerations: The power under Section 482 of the Code is to be used sparingly and only for the purpose of preventing abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure ends of justice.
